proposals.title: Leflunomide relieves differentiation blockade in AML through on-target DHODH inhibition at rheumatoid-arthritis-relevant exposure
proposals.text:
Hypothesis title: Leflunomide relieves differentiation blockade in AML through on-target DHODH inhibition at rheumatoid-arthritis-relevant exposure.

The proposal is that leflunomide, whose original indication is rheumatoid arthritis and whose active metabolite is teriflunomide (approval status, indication, and human exposure ranges are unverified prior knowledge), inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase in differentiation-blocked acute myeloid leukemia blasts and induces myeloid differentiation. The context is primary human AML with morphologic or immunophenotypic differentiation arrest. The endpoint is myeloid maturation. Bulk cytotoxicity, leukemia-stem-cell depletion, and normal progenitor toxicity are scored separately so differentiation is distinguished from stem-cell eradication and from nonspecific killing.

Supported premises. Experimental DHODH inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in AML models and affects disease-related endpoints in the systems investigated, connecting this metabolic step to relief of differentiation blockade as an outcome distinct from nonspecific cell killing [S4]. That evidence does not establish that every approved drug affecting the pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity [S4]. Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the specimens studied frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2, and BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells [S1]. This motivates study of specific dependencies and does not establish a therapeutic window for an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor [S1]. Venetoclax with azacitidine is an established comparator connected to leukemia-stem-cell TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation changes, and those findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug; that combination is not the candidate [S3]. Residual cells after cytarabine were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed oxidative-metabolism and fatty-acid-oxidation-associated features, and altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings [S2]. Those model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound [S2].

Speculative bridges. Moving the differentiation phenotype from experimental DHODH inhibition [S4] to leflunomide is an assumption. This packet contains no AML measurement of teriflunomide uptake, DHODH occupancy, or maturation. The hypothesis assumes that unbound concentrations reached during rheumatoid arthritis treatment, still requiring verification, engage DHODH inside primary blasts, and that myeloid maturation, rather than nucleotide-starvation cytotoxicity alone, explains any fall in leukemic burden. A selectivity window versus normal hematopoietic progenitors is also assumed.

Alternative explanations. Marker gains could reflect selective loss of immature blasts and persistence of cells that were already mature. Possible non-DHODH activities of leflunomide are unverified prior knowledge and could yield a phenotype that uridine does not reverse. Blasts that import extracellular pyrimidines could bypass the enzyme. Oxidative-phosphorylation collapse would align the result with BCL-2-linked stem-cell metabolism [S1] and the venetoclax-azacitidine comparator [S3], a different mechanism from DHODH-dependent differentiation [S4]. Loss of cytarabine-residual cells could instead track the fatty-acid-oxidation-associated state in those models [S2].

Discriminating preclinical test. In primary AML samples with differentiation arrest, paired with normal CD34-positive hematopoietic cells, measure dihydroorotate accumulation, pyrimidine-nucleotide depletion, morphology, and myeloid surface-marker acquisition across concentrations anchored to independently verified human free teriflunomide levels. Uridine supplementation is the on-target rescue; reversal supports DHODH dependence [S4]. A parallel venetoclax exposure is only a mechanistic comparator, with oxidative-phosphorylation rate recorded so DHODH-linked differentiation is separated from BCL-2-linked suppression of oxidative phosphorylation [S1][S3]. In a cytarabine-residual assay motivated by the oxidative residual state [S2], classify remaining cells by maturation versus death, keeping that readout distinct from the ROS-low stem-cell population [S1]. Normal myeloid colony formation is the selectivity comparator. A xenograft, if used, would match exposure and prespecify human-cell maturation together with normal hematopoietic toxicity.

Falsifying observation. The claim is disconfirmed if verified clinically relevant free teriflunomide exposure produces neither uridine-reversible DHODH-pathway engagement nor increased myeloid differentiation in primary differentiation-blocked AML. It is disconfirmed if that exposure suppresses normal myeloid colony formation to a similar degree. It is disconfirmed if maturation markers rise only with venetoclax-like oxidative-phosphorylation collapse [S1][S3] and persist after uridine rescue, placing the effect outside on-target DHODH inhibition [S4].

Limitations. The packet supports a pathway-level differentiation effect of DHODH inhibition in the models tested [S4], not clinical activity, subtype coverage, or sufficient leflunomide exposure. Approval, the rheumatoid arthritis indication, protein binding, and unbound plasma concentrations remain unverified prior knowledge. Tissue nucleosides may lessen pyrimidine depletion seen in culture. Differentiation can increase circulating mature myeloid cells and complicate burden readouts. Stem-cell oxidative metabolism [S1], chemotherapy-residual oxidative metabolism [S2], and venetoclax-azacitidine observations [S3] bound interpretation and are not efficacy evidence for leflunomide.

proposals.title: Bedaquiline, an approved multidrug-resistant-tuberculosis drug, collapses ATP-synthase-dependent oxidative phosphorylation to selectively deplete ROS-low leukemia stem cells and cytarabine-resistant OXPHOS-high residual AML cells.
proposals.text:
HYPOTHESIS TITLE: Bedaquiline, an approved multidrug-resistant-tuberculosis drug, collapses ATP-synthase-dependent oxidative phosphorylation to selectively deplete ROS-low leukemia stem cells and cytarabine-resistant OXPHOS-high residual AML cells.

HYPOTHESIS STATEMENT
Bedaquiline (original indication: multidrug-resistant tuberculosis — recalled, unverified prior knowledge that must be checked, including any approval-program restrictions) will suppress ATP-linked respiration in the two OXPHOS-dependent AML populations documented in the packet, reduce functional leukemia stem cell (LSC) frequency, and act independently of BCL-2 expression, thereby complementing rather than duplicating venetoclax. It is not an established AML therapy, and venetoclax-based regimens are treated here only as comparators, not as discoveries.

SUPPORTED PREMISES (from the packet)
1. Premise A [S1]: In the studied specimens, quiescent, ROS-low AML cells showed elevated BCL-2 and dependence on oxidative phosphorylation; BCL-2 inhibition reduced OXPHOS and targeted quiescent LSCs. This establishes quiescent-LSC OXPHOS reliance.
2. Premise B [S2]: Cytarabine-resistant residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature LSCs yet still required oxidative metabolism, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked features. This establishes a second, bulk-residual OXPHOS dependency distinct from the S1 population.
3. Premise C [S3]: Venetoclax–azacitidine was clinically linked to disruption of LSC energy metabolism (TCA-cycle/OXPHOS effects), providing a validated mechanistic comparator and suggesting the OXPHOS node itself is a clinically benchmarkable vulnerability.

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES (assumptions requiring verification; not supported by the packet)
- Bridge 1: Bedaquiline's antibacterial target is mycobacterial F1F0 ATP synthase, and published reports I recall (unverified) suggest off-target inhibition of mammalian ATP synthase at concentrations approaching achievable human plasma exposure. If false, the entire hypothesis fails.
- Bridge 2: Direct complex-V inhibition would phenocopy the S1 metabolic collapse without requiring the high-BCL-2 state, so activity should persist in BCL-2-low or MCL-1-compensated cells, unlike venetoclax.
- Bridge 3: I recall (unverified) that normal quiescent hematopoietic stem cells are glycolysis-biased; if true, a selectivity margin might exist. S1 and S2 do not establish normal-HSC resistance.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS
- Any killing could be nonspecific mitochondrial poisons-like toxicity equally affecting normal CD34+ cells.
- Effects could reflect cardiac off-targets (I recall QT-prolongation liability for bedaquiline — unverified) rather than ATP-synthase engagement.
- If cells die via a differentiation program resembling DHODH inhibition [S4], the mechanism would be different from OXPHOS collapse; S4 is used only as a mechanistic contrast, not support.

DISCRIMINATING PRECLINICAL TEST STRATEGY
1. Metabolic engagement: dose–response respirometry (OCR/ECAR) in primary AML specimens sorted into ROS-low versus ROS-high fractions, with ATP measurements, compared head-to-head with normal donor CD34+ HSCs (normal-cell comparator).
2. Target validation: show ATP depletion and either phenocopy by an unrelated ATP-synthase inhibitor or rescue by engineered ATP-synthase variants; off-target cardiac testing (hERG, cardiomyocyte function) to define the therapeutic window.
3. BCL-2-independence test: compare BCL-2-high versus BCL-2-low/MCL-1-high AML models, including venetoclax-resistant lines (mechanistic comparator = venetoclax per S3). Bedaquiline should retain activity where venetoclax fails under Premise-B conditions.
4. In vivo: PDX models treated with cytarabine, then bedaquiline; quantify residual disease and LSC frequency by limiting dilution, benchmarked against venetoclax–azacitidine [S3].

FALSIFYING OBSERVATION
If bedaquiline kills bulk blasts and normal CD34+ HSCs equipotently, shows no OXPHOS-state-dependent selectivity at concentrations matching achievable plasma exposure, and fails to deplete LSC frequency in PDXs, the drug–mechanism–context relationship is refuted. Mere cytotoxicity correlating with BCL-2 levels identically to venetoclax (no complementarity) would also falsify Bridge 2.

LIMITATIONS
- All approval, exposure, ATP-synthase, and cardiac claims above are recalled prior knowledge, not packet-verified facts; they must be checked before any program.
- S1/S2 are model-based and cannot be generalized to every AML genotype; OXPHOS dependency may vary by subtype and co-therapy exposure.
- Murine pharmacokinetics, protein binding, and tissue penetration of bedaquiline may not translate; tuberculosis dosing schedules may not achieve sustained antileukemic exposure safely.
- Even success would position bedaquiline as an investigational complement to standard care, not a replacement, and would require rigorous normal-HSC and cardiac safety evidence.

proposals.title: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis drug, as a clinically achievable DHODH inhibitor for cytarabine-resistant oxidative-metabolic AML residual cells.
proposals.text:
Title: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis drug, as a clinically achievable DHODH inhibitor for cytarabine-resistant oxidative-metabolic AML residual cells.

1) Hypothesis and context.
The hypothesis is deliberately narrow. Teriflunomide (approved for relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis; identification as leflunomide's active metabolite is unverified prior knowledge requiring regulatory-labelling confirmation) can, at clinically achievable unbound concentrations, inhibit DHODH and force differentiation (S4 mechanism) specifically in the cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolic residual-cell state (S2). The novelty is not DHODH-based differentiation per se — that mechanism is established by S4 and by clinical-stage DHODH inhibitors (unverified prior knowledge: brequinar-class tool compounds are substantially more potent than teriflunomide) — but whether an approved drug's human pharmacokinetics reach on-target marrow exposure, and whether the combined insult of pyrimidine depletion plus partial respiratory electron-flux reduction tips the S2 residual state toward differentiation rather than survival.

2) Known landscape (labeled unverified prior knowledge, not packet evidence).
Reported teriflunomide DHODH IC50: sub-micromolar to low micromolar. Steady-state plasma at approved 14 mg/day: high total levels with >99% protein binding; whether unbound exposure reaches IC50 is the central open question. Prior leflunomide-in-AML reports may exist (possibly in PTEN-mutant contexts); the claim is repositioned from mechanism discovery to an exposure-feasibility test in a specific residual-cell context, which is the genuinely incremental contribution.

3) Supported premises (frozen packet evidence).
[S4] DHODH inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in experimental AML — mechanistic core. [S2] Cytarabine-resistant residual cells are not necessarily LSC-enriched but require oxidative metabolism with FAO features — defining the contextual niche. [S1] ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent LSCs depend on OXPHOS — motivating a stem-cell metabolic vulnerability. [S3] Venetoclax–azacitidine disrupts TCA/OXPHOS — the in-study mechanistic comparator.

4) Speculative bridges (assumptions, not packet evidence).
Bridge A: On-target exposure is achievable — the go/no-go gate: verified unbound steady-state ≥ published DHODH IC50; if below by >5-fold, deprioritize before experimental commitment. Bridge B: Differentiation effects generalize from potent tool compounds to the less potent approved drug. Bridge C (exploratory): Partial complex III electron-flux reduction contributes to fate change; pyrimidine depletion alone may suffice. Bridge D (exploratory): ROS-low, BCL-2-high LSCs undergo differentiation or loss of self-renewal — S4 shows bulk differentiation only; this LSC extension is speculative. Bridge E (exploratory): BCL-2 inhibition deepens the metabolic insult; side experiment with venetoclax as comparator.

5) Alternative explanations.
Off-target kinase effects (reported for this class, unverified prior knowledge); nonspecific pyrimidine-starvation killing without lineage conversion; dominant electron-flux effect rather than pyrimidine mechanism; salvage-pathway compensation blunting de novo depletion.

6) Discriminating preclinical strategy.
Step 0: Feasibility triage — verify DHODH IC50, steady-state plasma, protein binding from regulatory/pharmacokinetic sources; compute estimated unbound marrow exposure; apply go/no-go gate. Step 1: Confirm enzymatic IC50. Step 2: 15+ primary AML samples vs normal CD34+ progenitors; differentiation, apoptosis, CFU, LSC limiting-dilution; additionally profile salvage-pathway capacity (uridine phosphorylase activity, thymidine pools) to pre-stratify samples vulnerable to de novo pathway block versus those expected to be resistant. Step 3: On-target and mechanism-discriminative proof: uridine/pyrimidine rescue; DHODH knockdown; teriflunomide-resistant DHODH replacement; mechanistic arms separating pyrimidine from electron-flux contributions — succinate-driven respiration (bypasses DHODH/ubiquinone entry point), paired respirometry under matched pyrimidine rescue, catalytic-competent but CoQ-binding-defective DHODH construct. Predefined thresholds: uridine fully rescues all endpoints → electron-flux contribution refuted; succinate bypass fails to rescue → electron-flux contribution supported; concurrent dihydroorotate accumulation with partial uridine rescue → on-target but unresolved branching. Step 4: Cytarabine-resistant residual-state emulation (S2); venetoclax comparator arm (S3). Step 5: PDX PK/PD in vivo.

Falsifying observations (predefined thresholds):
(a) No differentiation-marker increase and no LSC-frequency reduction at achievable concentrations.
(b) Effects not rescued by uridine AND not phenocopied by DHODH knockdown → off-target rather than on-target.
(c) Normal CD34+ CFU-GM toxicity ≥ AML toxicity, eliminating the therapeutic window.
(d) No in vivo blast/LSC reduction despite confirmed on-target marrow pharmacodynamics.
(e) Step 0 gate failure: estimated unbound exposure < DHODH IC50 by >5-fold, deprioritizing the hypothesis.

Limitations.
Preclinical and model-based; exposure, approval, and potency details rest on unverified prior knowledge pending verification; AML heterogeneity limits generality; salvage-pathway compensation may blunt differentiation; the claim is an incremental exposure-feasibility test in a specific residual-cell context, not a new-mechanism discovery; direct prior teriflunomide/leflunomide-in-AML reports may predate or obviate this proposal.

proposals.title: Premature stress-kinase phosphorylation of Nup98 initiates nucleocytoplasmic transport failure upstream of TDP-43 mislocalization in ALS motor neurons.
proposals.text:
Improved research hypothesis

Title: Premature stress-kinase phosphorylation of Nup98 initiates nucleocytoplasmic transport failure upstream of TDP-43 mislocalization in ALS motor neurons.

Hypothesis and causal chain. In TDP-43-positive ALS motor neurons — C9orf72 expansion carriers first, with non-C9 sporadic disease treated as an open subgroup — an aberrantly activated, proline-directed stress kinase phosphorylates nucleoporin Nup98 at sites homologous to those used during mitotic pore disassembly. Premature phosphorylation weakens Nup98 association with the pore scaffold, yielding a measurable pore-composition signature (loss of retention of other nucleoporins) that precedes Ran-dependent import failure, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing, and cell death. Phosphorylation is the initiating event; TDP-43 pathology and transport-factor sequestration are downstream responses.

Supported premises. (1) TDP-43 pathology is physically linked to nuclear-pore/transport components, with pore abnormalities in ALS tissue [S1]. (2) C9orf72 expansion disrupts import and RanGAP localization, and transport manipulations modify phenotypes [S2], making transport failure a plausible disease node. (3) Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies impair import, deplete nuclear TDP-43, and cause death independently of stress granules [S3]. (4) Stress granules can sequester transport factors and impair transport [S4], defining the main alternative. No supplied source establishes a nucleoporin phosphorylation initiator.

Speculative bridges, explicitly gated (assumptions). That Nup98 carries mitotic-disassembly phosphosites and that stress kinases can re-phosphorylate it in post-mitotic neurons is unverified prior knowledge; the sites and kinase are unknown. Therefore every perturbational arm is gated on a preliminary phosphoproteomic mapping result (Arm 0). Because the initiating step is load-bearing, no phosphorylation, site, or kinase claim is treated as evidence. The precommitted default kinase candidate is a Cdk-family kinase (e.g., Cdk5, a neuronal proline-directed kinase); this candidate, its site targeting, and inhibitor specificity are unverified prior knowledge and serve only as an initial hypothesis if the mapped motif is S/TP.

Alternative explanations. (a) Sequestration-first: stress granules sequester Ran/import factors with no pore modification [S4]. (b) TDP-43-first: cytoplasmic assemblies physically displace pore components, with phosphorylation secondary [S1, S3]. (c) Generic collapse: broad energetic/proteostatic stress with nonspecific phosphorylation.

Discriminating strategy. Systems: iPSC-derived motor neurons from C9orf72 ALS patients and non-C9 sporadic ALS patients with TDP-43 pathology, isogenic CRISPR-corrected controls, and an acute stress model.

Arm 0 (gating and specificity): time-resolved phosphoproteomics of enriched pore fractions with phospho-specific antibodies to mapped Nup98 sites, tracked in parallel with live NLS-GFP import kinetics, RanGAP localization, and endogenous TDP-43 localization. Simultaneously record global-stress readouts (stress/translation markers and a panel of unrelated phosphosites) to show Nup98 phosphorylation is specific, not a bystander of cellular collapse, excluding alternative (c). Prediction: Nup98 phosphorylation rises before import decline and nuclear TDP-43 loss. All later arms proceed only if this gate passes.

Arm 1 (necessity, deconfounded editing): inducible, post-differentiation knock-in of non-phosphorylatable Nup98 (S-to-A) at mapped sites in already post-mitotic motor neurons, avoiding pre-mitotic editing that could impair mitotic pore disassembly, cell fitness, and cloning. Controls: cell fitness and NPC composition. Prediction: rescued import and reduced TDP-43 mislocalization despite repeats or stress.

Arm 2 (sufficiency, not mimic-dependent): S-to-D/E knock-in is included but treated as a weak mimic that may fail structurally. Orthogonal sufficiency: inducible recruitment of the candidate kinase (or inducible phosphatase interference) to the nuclear pore in healthy control neurons. Prediction: either manipulation alone induces import failure and nuclear TDP-43 depletion without stress or pre-existing aggregation. A negative phosphomimetic alone would not falsify the hypothesis.

Arm 3 (conditional staged inhibition): only after Arm 0 fixes one kinase-inhibitor pair via mapped phosphosite motif and in vitro kinase screening, apply early versus late inhibition, paired with genetic tools (kinase knockdown/kinase-dead) and off-target controls. Prediction: early inhibition rescues transport and prevents TDP-43 mislocalization; late inhibition after de-mixing does not.

Arm 4 (sequestration discrimination, [S4]): repeat assays in stress-granule-blocked neurons (e.g., G3BP1/2 loss; perturbation rationale unverified prior knowledge), plus a head-to-head comparison of transport signatures — pore-composition imaging of other Nups' retention and cargo-selective import assays — to separate scaffold weakening from import-factor sequestration. Prediction: persistent import impairment with a pore-composition signature under Nup98 phosphorylation; pure sequestration predicts rescue with preserved pore composition.

Arm 5 (TDP-43-first discrimination, [S1, S3]): block cytoplasmic assembly using temporally controlled aggregation-defective TDP-43 variants (unverified prior knowledge), not nuclear-restricted TDP-43, which itself alters RNA metabolism and would confound the test. Prediction: early Nup98 phosphorylation and import loss persist even when cytoplasmic assembly is blocked.

Falsifying observation. The hypothesis is falsified if import failure and nuclear TDP-43 loss precede detectable Nup98 phosphorylation in time-resolved assays; if post-mitotic non-phosphorylatable knock-in fails to rescue while stress-granule disruption rescues; or if the orthogonal pore-targeted kinase/phosphatase-arm fails to impair transport. Any such outcome demotes phosphorylation to a downstream marker at best.

Limitations. Phosphosite detection in scarce motor-neuron material may lack depth; if Arm 0 fails, the hypothesis stalls untested at the perturbational level; iPSC neurons do not reproduce decades of aging; kinase selection could be wrong despite motif screening; cell-level rescue demonstrates necessity and sufficiency only in vitro, not initiation in patients; subtype heterogeneity is unresolved.

proposals.title: Teriflunomide-induced differentiation of pyrimidine-salvage-poor residual AML after cytarabine
proposals.text:
Teriflunomide-induced differentiation of pyrimidine-salvage-poor residual AML after cytarabine

Hypothesis. At human-attainable unbound exposure, teriflunomide will inhibit DHODH, induce durable myeloid differentiation, and reduce leukemia-propagating activity in cytarabine-residual, oxidative AML unable to compensate through pyrimidine salvage, while preserving normal progenitor function. The speculative bridges are inadequate adaptive salvage, maturation rather than arrest or death, and a selective exposure window.

Supported premises. Cytarabine-resistant AML cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties without consistent enrichment for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells [S2]. DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation in experimental AML [S4]. Neither finding establishes DHODH dependence in oxidative residual disease. ROS-low, BCL-2-associated leukemia stem cells constitute a separately assessed population [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is an established metabolic comparator, not this repurposing proposal [S3]. Bulk killing, differentiation, and loss of leukemia-propagating activity remain distinct endpoints.

Drug-specific uncertainties. Unverified prior knowledge identifies teriflunomide as approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis, a DHODH inhibitor, and substantially protein-bound; it also links DHODH to de novo pyrimidine synthesis and uridine to salvage. These recollections require verification. Before translational testing, confirm approval and original indication, biochemical and cellular potency, protein binding, human pharmacokinetics, and documented hematopoietic toxicity. Measure free drug in the experimental medium rather than extrapolating from total plasma concentrations.

Quantitative exposure gate. Establish numerical human unbound Cmax and AUC ceilings from verified, tolerable labeled dosing before efficacy experiments. Translational concentration–time profiles must have unbound Cmax and AUC ratios no greater than 1 relative to those ceilings, with an experimental entry criterion of at least 50% DHODH inhibition. These are protocol gates, not validated efficacy thresholds. The packet cannot supply absolute exposure values; failure to engage DHODH within these bounds stops the translational claim. Marrow exposure requires separate measurement.

Incremental contribution. DHODH-driven differentiation is already supported [S4]; neither that mechanism nor first teriflunomide use in AML is claimed as novel. Prior teriflunomide/leflunomide AML studies require checking because they are absent from the packet. The proposed increment is adaptive-salvage stratification in post-cytarabine disease, with comparison against a validated selective DHODH inhibitor.

Prospective population definition. Use paired pretreatment/post-cytarabine specimens and independently derived residual-disease models. Low baseline salvage flux is insufficient: in separate classification aliquots, measure isotope-resolved de novo and salvage flux before and 24–48 hours after reference DHODH blockade under measured physiological uridine and protein conditions. Provisionally classify salvage-poor samples as maintaining UTP at no more than 50% of vehicle at both time points despite adaptation, and competent samples as recovering to at least 80%; analyze intermediate values continuously. These prespecified conventions require robustness testing. Define oxidative-high/low groups using reference-cohort, viable-cell-normalized oxygen-consumption tertiles. Factorially compare both oxidative groups and both salvage classes to determine whether oxidative status adds predictive value.

Discriminating experiments. Compare vehicle, teriflunomide, a biochemically validated selective DHODH inhibitor, and inducible partial DHODH suppression at matched target engagement. Measure intracellular exposure, pyrimidine pools, flux, and target inhibition before substantial cell loss. Test validated gain/loss perturbations of uridine uptake or phosphorylation: increasing functional salvage should attenuate differentiation and propagation loss, whereas reducing salvage should sensitize competent cells. Confirm flux changes rather than relying on expression. Uridine rescue is interpretable only when uptake is demonstrated and does not establish unique target specificity. An independently validated, catalytically functional teriflunomide-insensitive DHODH rescue would strengthen attribution. Include venetoclax–azacitidine [S3], untreated AML, and normal donor progenitors.

Functional outcomes and alternatives. Track initially immature, genotype-confirmed leukemic cells with lineage labels, morphology, and maturation markers to distinguish induced differentiation from survival of pre-existing mature cells. Measure apoptosis separately. After verified drug clearance, assess clonogenic recovery and transplantation-based leukemia initiation. Exposure-matched xenografts should measure marrow pharmacology; normal-progenitor colony formation and engraftment test selectivity. Off-target toxicity, reversible arrest, chemotherapy-associated oxidative stress, and culture-induced uridine scarcity remain alternative explanations addressed by orthogonal perturbations, longitudinal tracking, and physiological conditions.

Falsification and limitations. Confirmed DHODH inhibition and pyrimidine depletion within exposure bounds, without differentiation or reduced propagation in preclassified salvage-poor residual AML, would falsify the central mechanism–context prediction. Failure of verified salvage manipulation to alter response would reject salvage as the causal stratifier. Comparable normal-progenitor impairment would reject selectivity; activity only above human exposure bounds would reject translation. Heterogeneity, unstable salvage adaptation, transplantation biases, uncertain marrow exposure, and overlapping prior work limit interpretation. Positive preclinical findings would not establish clinical efficacy.

proposals.title: Premature stress-kinase phosphorylation of Nup98 initiates nucleocytoplasmic transport failure upstream of TDP-43 mislocalization in ALS motor neurons
proposals.text:
Title: Premature stress-kinase phosphorylation of Nup98 initiates nucleocytoplasmic transport failure upstream of TDP-43 mislocalization in ALS motor neurons.

Hypothesis and causal chain. In TDP-43-positive ALS motor neurons, including but not limited to C9orf72 expansion carriers, an aberrantly activated stress-associated kinase phosphorylates the nucleoporin Nup98 at sites normally used only during mitotic pore disassembly. This premature phosphorylation weakens Nup98 association with the pore scaffold, causing partial nuclear-pore destabilization and early import failure. Collapsed Ran-dependent import then prevents nuclear retention of TDP-43, driving nuclear TDP-43 depletion, cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing, and ultimately cell death. Under this hypothesis, nucleoporin phosphorylation is the initiating event; TDP-43 pathology and aggregate-associated sequestration are downstream responses.

Supported premises. (1) TDP-43 pathology is physically linked to nuclear-pore and transport components, with pore abnormalities observed in ALS tissue [S1]. (2) C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nuclear import and RanGAP localization, and transport-related perturbations modify model phenotypes [S2], confirming that transport failure is a plausible disease-relevant node. (3) Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies impair import, deplete nuclear TDP-43, and cause cell death independently of conventional stress granules [S3], establishing that transport failure and TDP-43 mislocalization are mechanistically coupled. (4) Stress granules can sequester transport factors and impair transport [S4], defining the main alternative class of mechanism. None of S1-S4 establishes a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as an initiating cause; that step is purely hypothesized.

Speculative bridges (assumptions, not evidence). The identity of the kinase is an assumption; from recalled, unverified prior knowledge, mitotic kinases such as Cdk-family kinases phosphorylate Nup98 during pore disassembly, and Cdk5 or MAPK-family stress kinases could aberrantly reactivate such programs in post-mitotic neurons. The specific Nup98 phosphorylation sites are unknown and must be mapped. The direction of causality (phosphorylation preceding TDP-43 mislocalization) is the hypothesis itself, not established fact. Whether the mechanism operates in sporadic ALS, C9orf72 ALS, or both is open; the hypothesis is deliberately restricted to TDP-43-positive contexts and makes no universal claim.

Alternative explanations. (a) Sequestration-first: stress granules sequester Ran and import factors, impairing transport without any pore modification [S4]. (b) TDP-43-first: cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies physically pull pore or transport components out of position, with phosphorylation appearing only secondarily [S1, S3]. (c) Generic collapse: broad energetic or proteostatic stress secondarily degrades transport with no specific pore phosphorylation.

Discriminating preclinical strategy. Use iPSC-derived motor neurons from C9orf72 ALS patients and non-C9 sporadic ALS patients with TDP-43 pathology, plus isogenic CRISPR-corrected controls, and an acute stress model. First, temporal mapping: time-resolved phosphoproteomics of enriched pore fractions and phospho-specific antibodies against mapped Nup98 sites, tracked in parallel with live imaging of NLS-GFP import kinetics, RanGAP localization, and endogenous TDP-43 localization. The hypothesis predicts Nup98 phosphorylation rises before measurable import decline and before nuclear TDP-43 loss. Second, perturbational necessity: CRISPR knock-in of non-phosphorylatable Nup98 (S-to-A) at candidate sites should rescue import defects and reduce TDP-43 mislocalization despite C9orf72 repeats or stress. Third, perturbational sufficiency: phospho-mimetic knock-in (S-to-D/E) in control neurons should alone induce import failure and nuclear TDP-43 depletion without stress or pre-existing TDP-43 aggregation. Fourth, staged kinase inhibition: blocking the suspected kinase early should rescue transport and prevent TDP-43 mislocalization, whereas late inhibition after aggregate formation should not. Fifth, discrimination from the sequestration alternative [S4]: repeat the assays in neurons where stress-granule assembly is blocked (for example via G3BP1/2 loss; this perturbation rationale is unverified prior knowledge); the hypothesis predicts persistent import impairment if Nup98 phosphorylation occurs, whereas pure sequestration predicts rescue. Sixth, discrimination from the TDP-43-first alternative [S1, S3]: prevent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assembly or express nuclear-restricted TDP-43; the hypothesis predicts early Nup98 phosphorylation and import loss even when cytoplasmic aggregation is blocked.

Falsifying observation. The hypothesis is falsified if import failure and nuclear TDP-43 loss precede detectable Nup98 phosphorylation in time-resolved assays; if non-phosphorylatable Nup98 knock-in fails to rescue transport while stress-granule disruption rescues it; or if phospho-mimetic Nup98 produces no transport defect in otherwise healthy motor neurons. Any of these outcomes would demote phosphorylation to a downstream marker at best.

Limitations. Phosphosite detection in scarce motor-neuron material may lack depth; iPSC motor neurons may not reproduce decades-long aging dynamics; the kinase could differ across ALS subtypes; model rescue demonstrates necessity and sufficiency in cells, not that phosphorylation initiates disease in patients.

proposals.title: CDK5-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation initiates nuclear-import failure in TARDBP-associated ALS
proposals.text:
CDK5-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation initiates nuclear-import failure in TARDBP-associated ALS

Hypothesis. In mature motor neurons carrying pathogenic TARDBP variants, impaired calcium clearance activates a calcium–calpain–p35/p25–CDK5 pathway. CDK5-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation reduces its pore residence, causing import failure before detectable cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies. Nuclear TDP-43 depletion then contributes to firing deficits and death. This initiating chain is proposed, not established. “Initiating” means upstream of transport failure, not the inherited variant; the scope is TARDBP-associated ALS.

Evidence and candidate-selection gap. Disease-linked TDP-43 can disrupt nucleoporin localization and transport [S1]. Cytoplasmic assemblies can impair import without conventional stress granules [S3], whereas stress-granule sequestration supplies an alternative [S4]. C9orf72-associated RanGAP abnormalities provide another genetic-context-specific route [S2]. None establishes nucleoporin phosphorylation; phosphorylated TDP-43 is not evidence of phosphorylated NUP98 [S3]. Unverified prior knowledge motivates candidate selection: TDP-43 participates in RNA regulation, calcium-dependent calpain cleavage of p35 to p25 can deregulate CDK5, and mitotic phosphorylation can promote NUP98 release from pores. The speculative bridges are altered RNA regulation impairing calcium handling, direct CDK5 modification of NUP98, and transfer of phosphorylation-sensitive pore release to postmitotic neurons. These precedents motivate selection but do not establish this pairing or literature-wide novelty.

Longitudinal strategy and decision rules. Use multiple donor-derived TARDBP motor-neuron lines, isogenic corrections, independent differentiations, and blinded analyses without imposed global stress. Measure calcium-clearance kinetics, calpain activity, p25:p35, CDK5 activity, NUP98 phosphosite occupancy, endogenous NUP98 pore residence by single-particle tracking, kinetic import, export, passive permeability, TDP-43 localization/assemblies, stress granules, firing, energy status, and survival. Discovery cultures identify reproducible early phosphosites; lock sites and endpoints before independent confirmation. Preregister ≥20% import-rate impairment and ≥50% closure of mutant–corrected import and firing deficits as operational impairment/rescue thresholds. Require upstream calcium/p25/CDK5 changes before phosphorylation, phosphorylation before residence loss, and both pore changes ≥24 hours before import failure and detectable assemblies.

Modification causality. In mature neurons, compare calpain inhibition and cleavage-resistant p35 replacement, with matched-expression p25 bypass, to test the proposed upstream trigger. Acute CDK5 suppression with active-versus-inactive kinase rescue tests kinase dependence; purified CDK5 must modify the same locked sites. Endogenous phosphoresistant NUP98 editing and inducible NUP98-targeted phosphatase recruitment provide orthogonal modification tests. Include wild-type edits and inactive-phosphatase controls, and verify unchanged neighboring nucleoporin phosphorylation, NUP98 abundance, maturation, baseline pore architecture, and basal transport. Phosphoresistance should preserve import and neuronal function while occluding additional CDK5-dependent protection.

Pore and transport mediation. Site-dependent rescue alone cannot establish displacement as the mediator. Inducibly tether NUP98 to a localization-validated NUP93 pore anchor, with anchor-only and tether-defective controls. Require restored residence while nominated phosphosites remain phosphorylated and baseline pore function remains normal. Rescue under these conditions would support displacement-mediated failure rather than other NUP98 functions. Joint rescue still does not establish transport mediation: after tether rescue, titrated inducible importin-β depletion should reproduce the original import deficit and eliminate neuronal protection without changing NUP98 residence. Interpret this only before generalized injury develops.

Alternative discrimination. Factorially compare NUP98 interventions with candidate assembly suppressors. Nominated from unverified prior knowledge, use G3BP1/2 CRISPRi versus ISRIB for conventional granules, and HSPB8 induction versus an engineered assembly-selective TDP-43 intrabody for nongranular assemblies. Their selectivity is not assumed. Interpret only independently validated conditions reducing targeted assemblies by ≥50%, preserving TDP-43 abundance and splicing function, and not independently changing CDK5 activity, basal import, calcium, energy status, or stress in pre-defect controls. Include non-targeting and inactive-binder controls; failed validation makes an arm inconclusive. The pore mechanism predicts early phosphorylation, residence loss, and import failure persist despite validated assembly suppression. Restoration of import despite persistent phosphorylation and residence loss instead favors sequestration. Blocking conventional granules alone cannot exclude the route in [S3].

Falsification and limitations. Verified prevention of the locked phosphorylation events that leaves early import failure and neuronal dysfunction unchanged falsifies their necessary initiating role, especially if assembly suppression restores transport. Phosphorylation appearing only after import failure contradicts the temporal claim. Successful retention with preserved phosphorylation but no import rescue rejects displacement as the mediator. Undetected small assemblies, unresolved RNA-to-calcium linkage, artificial tethering, phosphatase spillover, editing artifacts, and kinase pleiotropy remain limitations. Transport re-blocking accompanied by broad injury cannot resolve mediation. Findings would remain preclinical and TARDBP-context-specific, not a validated treatment.

proposals.title: CDK5-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation as an initiating nuclear-import defect in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons
proposals.text:
CDK5-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation as an initiating nuclear-import defect in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons

Hypothesis. In human motor neurons carrying an ALS-associated TARDBP mutation, excessive CDK5-dependent phosphorylation of NUP98’s FG-repeat region reduces NUP98 retention at nuclear pores, initiating impaired nuclear import before nuclear TDP-43 depletion, persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies, and neuronal dysfunction. This proposes an initiating transport lesion within a defined ALS context—not the original cause of ALS or a universal mechanism across subtypes.

Supported premises. Disease-linked TDP-43 can disrupt nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport, and related pore pathology occurs in ALS tissue [S1]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can recruit or mislocalize transport-associated proteins alongside import impairment, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death, without requiring conventional stress granules [S3]. Stress granules provide another route by sequestering transport factors [S4]. C9orf72-repeat-associated disruption of RanGAP localization and import establishes a distinct genetic-context-specific transport defect, not evidence for this proposed TARDBP–NUP98 pathway [S2]. None of these sources establishes nucleoporin phosphorylation as an initiating lesion.

Speculative bridges. Unverified prior knowledge motivates choosing NUP98 as an FG-repeat nucleoporin and CDK5 as a neuron-relevant kinase. The packet does not establish their biochemical relationship. Direct CDK5 phosphorylation of NUP98, its disease-associated increase, altered pore retention, and the resulting import defect are explicit assumptions. The proposed downstream progression from impaired import to TDP-43 redistribution and dysfunction is also unproven in this context. Phosphorylation could instead stabilize damaged pores or simply mark cellular stress.

Discriminating preclinical strategy. Study independently derived TARDBP-mutant induced-pluripotent-stem-cell motor neurons with isogenic corrected controls, using matched longitudinal cultures before overt degeneration. Measure pore-associated NUP98 phosphorylation by targeted phosphoproteomics, NUP98 pore localization, nuclear-import kinetics with a standardized reporter, nuclear and cytoplasmic TDP-43, conventional stress-granule formation, transport-factor partitioning, axonal integrity, and survival. Import kinetics—not merely a steady-state nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio—should be the primary early endpoint. The predicted order is increased NUP98 phosphorylation, reduced pore residence, impaired import, then TDP-43 redistribution and dysfunction.

Map reproducibly increased phosphorylation sites within the prespecified NUP98 region, and test whether purified CDK5 can phosphorylate those same sites directly. Genetic CDK5 suppression, with rescue by active versus kinase-inactive CDK5, would test kinase dependence. Introduce endogenous nonphosphorylatable substitutions at the mapped sites alongside matched wild-type editing controls; verify comparable NUP98 expression, differentiation, and basal pore function. Protection should preserve early import despite the TARDBP mutation and without reducing upstream stress. For a sufficiency test, inducible CDK5 activation in corrected neurons should reproduce the sequence when NUP98 is phosphorylatable but not in the baseline-functional nonphosphorylatable background. This comparison is essential because CDK5 manipulation alone could affect many other substrates.

Alternatives and discrimination. Transport-factor sequestration by stress granules [S4] or stress-granule-independent TDP-43 assemblies [S3] could cause import failure first, with NUP98 phosphorylation appearing secondarily. Broader stress could independently produce both events. Measure these processes concurrently and perturb conventional stress-granule assembly in parallel. Stress-granule suppression alone cannot exclude the assembly route in S3. The phosphorylation hypothesis specifically requires early import protection by NUP98 phosphosite editing before changes in assembly burden, with comparable upstream stress and viability. Rescue occurring only after reduced sequestration would favor an alternative explanation. Temporal precedence without this site-specific intervention would be insufficient.

Falsifying observation. If baseline-functional NUP98 phosphosite editing abolishes the proposed phosphorylation event but leaves the earliest import defect unchanged under matched stress and viability, the claimed initiating mechanism is falsified—even if later neuronal survival improves.

Limitations. Relevant sites remain unknown, and substitutions may alter NUP98 independently of phosphorylation. Direct biochemical phosphorylation does not establish neuronal causality. Cultured motor-neuron maturation, kinase pleiotropy, and ALS heterogeneity constrain interpretation. Any positive result would establish a restricted preclinical mechanism, not a validated treatment or a general explanation of ALS.

proposals.title: ERK2 phosphorylation of pore-resident FG-nucleoporin Nup62 at Ser59, Ser84, Ser178, and Ser221 initiates selective NLS-import failure and nuclear TDP-43 loss downstream of cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing in TDP-43 proteinopathy models of ALS
proposals.text:
Hypothesis. ERK2 phosphorylation of pore-resident FG-nucleoporin Nup62 at Ser59, Ser84, Ser178, and Ser221 initiates selective NLS-import failure and nuclear TDP-43 loss downstream of cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing in TDP-43 proteinopathy models of ALS.

The setting is neuronal TDP-43 proteinopathy. C9orf72 repeat disease is a comparison arm. SOD1-linked disease and unselected sporadic ALS stay outside this claim. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing is the upstream condition. Phosphorylation at these sites is the pore-intrinsic step that initiates selective NLS-import failure and nuclear TDP-43 loss. Neuronal death is a later response. ERK2 (MAPK1) is the single assumed kinase. Ser59, Ser84, Ser178, and Ser221 are the stipulated site list, fixed before outcome data. Unverified prior knowledge only motivates an FG-region focus and the use of scaffold nucleoporin Nup107 as an occupancy normalizer. That background lies outside [S1]–[S4] and carries no citation identifier.

Supported premises come from the packet. Nuclear-pore and transport components associate with insoluble TDP-43, disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in cells, and related pore pathology occurs in ALS tissue [S1]. Expanded C9orf72 RNA is linked to RanGAP mislocalization and impaired nuclear import, and transport or repeat-RNA manipulations can modify those model phenotypes [S2]. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can form without conventional stress granules, mislocalize transport-associated proteins, and accompany import failure, nuclear TDP-43 loss, and cell death; phosphorylated TDP-43 in those assemblies documents TDP-43 phosphorylation [S3]. Cellular stress can recruit transport factors into stress granules and impair transport, and changing stress-granule assembly can modify those defects [S4]. The packet supplies no nucleoporin phosphorylation event as a cause.

Speculative bridges. After de-mixing has begun, assumed ERK2 phosphorylates pore-resident Nup62 at the four stipulated sites. The assumed effect is weaker FG-repeat cohesion and slower facilitated import of NLS cargo, including TDP-43, while a size-matched non-NLS reporter keeps its nuclear-entry rate. Nuclear TDP-43 depletion follows that import defect. Because [S1] documents nucleoporin mislocalization, the bridge applies only while Nup62 remains in the NPC fraction.

Alternatives remain fully viable. Stress granules may sequester transport factors and impair transport [S4]. Stress-granule-independent assemblies may capture transport factors and nucleoporins [S1, S3]. C9orf72 repeat RNA and RanGAP mislocalization may drive import failure on their own [S2]. Broader Ran-gradient or energetic failure may impair transport after injury is underway.

Discriminating test. Human iPSC-derived motor neurons are studied in three arms: cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing with a low stress-granule burden [S3]; acute stress-granule induction [S4]; and C9orf72 repeat-RNA expression [S2]. The claim is mediator status after de-mixing. An assembly-free phospho-mimetic result is uninformative for this claim. Phospho-mimetic Nup62 is used only in the de-mixing arm, as an augmentation probe under that upstream condition. Time points are 0, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h. Endpoints are mean four-site phospho-stoichiometry, Nup62/Nup107 in the same fraction, NLS-reporter import rate, size-matched non-NLS reporter rate, nuclear-to-cytoplasmic TDP-43 ratio, G3BP1 area, cytoplasmic TDP-43 assembly burden, RanGAP localization, and a death marker. NPC fractions are nuclear envelopes from sequential detergent extraction. Stoichiometry is phospho/(phospho+unmodified) by parallel-reaction monitoring with stable-isotope AQUA peptides limited to Ser59, Ser84, Ser178, and Ser221. The prespecified endpoint is the mean of those four occupancies. Endogenous Nup62 is replaced by alanine or aspartate substitutions at only those residues. A corroborative arm combines ERK2 knockdown with a second, chemically distinct ERK2 inhibitor. Allele replacement is decisive.

Support thresholds in the de-mixing arm. Assembly burden reaches at least 2-fold at t_a. Mean phospho-occupancy then rises by at least 0.15 while Nup62/Nup107 remains at least 70% of baseline at t_p. At least 2 h later, NLS import falls by at least 40% and the non-NLS rate changes by less than 15%. The TDP-43 nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio then falls by at least 30%, and the death marker rises only afterward. Phospho-deficient Nup62 holds the NLS-import change under 15% and the TDP-43-ratio change under 15%, with assemblies still at least 2-fold, G3BP1 area within 20% of matched de-mixing cells, and Nup62/Nup107 at least 70%. Phospho-mimetic Nup62, still under de-mixing, deepens the NLS-import deficit by at least 25 percentage points. In the C9orf72 arm the alanine replacement restores at most 15 percentage points of the NLS deficit. Rescue confined to cultures whose G3BP1 area falls by at least 50% favors sequestration [S3, S4]. A requirement confined to the repeat-RNA arm favors the C9orf72 route [S2].

Falsifying observations. Each result rejects the initiating-pore claim on its own. The claim is rejected if NLS import falls by at least 40% and the TDP-43 ratio falls by at least 30% while mean four-site occupancy has risen by less than 0.15, including when Nup62/Nup107 remains at least 70%. The claim is rejected if phospho-deficient Nup62 leaves an NLS-import drop of at least 40% and a TDP-43-ratio drop of at least 30% intact, with assemblies still at least 2-fold and Nup62/Nup107 at least 70%. The selective-import claim is rejected if the non-NLS rate rises by at least 40% in the same window as the NLS drop. The pore-resident claim is rejected if Nup62/Nup107 falls below 70% of baseline before occupancy rises by 0.15 and import still fails.

Limitations. ERK2, the four residue numbers, the FG-region assignment, and the Nup107 normalizer are assumptions. Unverified background is not packet evidence. The AQUA panel stays restricted to those four residues for the life of the study; unmodified sites falsify this locked target. Phospho-mimetic side chains approximate phosphate and speak only under continued de-mixing. Phosphorylation of other nucleoporins could mask a single-protein effect. iPSC motor neurons omit aging, glia, and circuit context. ERK2 inhibitors have off-target actions. The design tests a research hypothesis and stops short of a treatment claim.

proposals.title: CDK5-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation as an initiating nuclear-import defect in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons
proposals.text:
CDK5-dependent NUP98 phosphorylation as an initiating nuclear-import defect in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons

Hypothesis. In heterozygous TARDBP-M337V human motor neurons, increased endogenous CDK5 activity phosphorylates NUP98’s FG-repeat region, shortening pore residence and initiating impaired nuclear import before nuclear TDP-43 depletion, persistent cytoplasmic assemblies, and neuronal dysfunction. This proposes a proximal initiating transport lesion, not the origin of ALS or a universal mechanism. The allele’s ALS association is unverified prior knowledge; this causal chain is speculative.

Supported premises. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and transport, with related pore pathology in ALS tissue [S1]. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can recruit transport-associated proteins alongside import impairment, nuclear depletion, and death without conventional stress granules [S3]. Conventional stress granules provide another sequestration route [S4]. C9orf72-associated RanGAP/import defects establish a separate genetic-context-specific mechanism [S2], not evidence for this phosphorylation pathway. None establishes nucleoporin phosphorylation as an initiating lesion.

Speculative substrate rationale. Unverified prior knowledge motivates CDK5 as a neuron-relevant, proline-directed kinase and NUP98 as an FG nucleoporin. The FG-region choice assumes phosphorylation alters interactions controlling pore retention. No packet evidence favors this pairing over another kinase or anchoring-domain modification. Map early mutant-enriched FG-region phosphosites and test motif compatibility. Measure endogenous CDK5 activity, abundance, and regulatory-complex association before import divergence. Compare competing neuronal kinases against the same sites; purified CDK5 must phosphorylate them directly. Missing sites or absent CDK5 dependence would reject this pairing, not justify substituting another mechanism.

Temporal and pore-specific tests. Use multiple independently derived mutant/corrected isogenic iPSC motor-neuron pairs and sham-edited controls. Require a documented normal-import baseline after motor-neuron specification; pre-degeneration sampling alone cannot establish initiation. Track phosphosite occupancy, pore-resolved photoconversion kinetics of endogenously tagged NUP98, import kinetics, TDP-43 distribution, assemblies, transport-factor partitioning, stress, axonal integrity, and survival. Reconstitute import in semi-permeabilized neurons with identical soluble transport machinery and energy, verifying phosphorylation retention, comparable Ran gradients, and envelope integrity. Include passive-permeability and export controls. Persistent impairment supports a pore-retained defect; disappearance favors soluble-factor depletion rather than proving intrinsic pore failure.

Substrate-specific causality and mediation. Test CDK5 dependence by genetic suppression with active versus kinase-inactive rescue. Introduce endogenous nonphosphorylatable substitutions at mapped sites, requiring normal expression, differentiation, and basal transport against wild-type editing controls. In corrected neurons, CDK5 activation matched to mutant activity should reproduce the residence/import sequence with phosphorylatable NUP98 but not the functional nonphosphorylatable background. Kinase manipulation or phosphosite rescue alone cannot establish residence mediation. Independently restore NUP98 residence using an inducible pore-targeted tether calibrated to normal dwell times, with anchor-only and wild-type-tether controls. Import rescue despite persistent phosphorylation would support residence as mediator. Site-edit rescue without residence restoration would instead undermine that causal link. Evaluate early protection before assembly burden changes, with matched upstream stress and viability.

Alternative-pathway discrimination. Monitoring stress-granule-independent assemblies is insufficient. Alongside conventional stress-granule suppression [S4], develop and prevalidate a cytoplasm-restricted, assembly-disrupting TDP-43 intrabody as a candidate intervention against S3-type sequestration. Require reduced assemblies and assembly-associated transport-factor partitioning, unchanged total TDP-43, and normal basal nuclear TDP-43 and import in corrected controls. Reject the reagent if it directly alters CDK5 or NUP98; include an inactive binder and verify comparable upstream stress. Apply interventions before divergence and after assemblies appear. The hypothesis predicts that suppressing sequestration will not prevent the first phosphorylation/residence/import defect, whereas NUP98 editing will prevent import failure before changing assemblies. Assembly suppression preventing early phosphorylation and import failure would favor sequestration-first causation. Phosphorylation appearing only after import failure would favor a downstream response. Broader stress independently causing both remains an alternative; timing alone cannot exclude it.

Falsifying observation. If baseline-functional phosphosite edits abolish the mapped CDK5-dependent phosphorylation event but leave the earliest import defect unchanged under matched stress and viability, the claimed initiating mechanism is falsified—even if later survival improves.

Limitations. A sufficiently selective assembly intervention may not be achievable; without validated specificity, that comparison is inconclusive. Editing, tagging, permeabilization, and tethering can independently perturb pores. Biochemical phosphorylation does not establish neuronal causality. Temporal resolution, kinase pleiotropy, cultured-neuron immaturity, and allele specificity limit inference. Positive findings would establish a restricted preclinical mechanism, not a validated treatment.

proposals.title: Teriflunomide-induced differentiation of pyrimidine-salvage-poor residual AML after cytarabine
proposals.text:
Teriflunomide-induced differentiation of pyrimidine-salvage-poor residual AML after cytarabine

Hypothesis: At clinically attainable unbound exposure, teriflunomide will inhibit DHODH and induce durable myeloid differentiation in cytarabine-residual AML cells that retain oxidative metabolism but have insufficient pyrimidine-salvage capacity. This will reduce leukemia-propagating activity while preserving normal hematopoietic progenitor function. The proposed context is functionally defined residual disease, not all AML or an assumed leukemia-stem-cell population.

Supported premises: Cytarabine-resistant AML cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties but were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells [S2]. Separately, DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation in experimental AML systems [S4]. These findings justify testing a metabolic differentiation strategy in residual disease, but do not establish that oxidative residual cells depend on DHODH. ROS-low leukemia stem cells and their BCL-2-associated metabolic vulnerability represent a distinct population requiring separate functional assessment [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine provides an established energy-metabolism comparator, not the proposed repurposing discovery [S3].

Unverified prior knowledge: Teriflunomide is recalled as an approved treatment for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis and as a DHODH inhibitor with substantial plasma-protein binding. These approval, original-indication, pharmacology, and binding facts require independent verification because the packet does not establish them. Human exposure, marrow penetration, and safety constraints likewise need checking before translational interpretation. No first-in-AML discovery claim is made.

Speculative bridges: The proposal assumes that a subset of oxidative residual AML relies sufficiently on de novo pyrimidine synthesis that DHODH inhibition cannot be compensated by salvage. It further assumes that teriflunomide can engage this dependency at tolerable exposure and that nucleotide restriction produces maturation rather than merely arrest or death. Oxidative metabolism would be an enrichment context, not a surrogate proof of DHODH dependence. Selectivity is a prediction to test, not an inference from the multiple-sclerosis indication or from [S4].

Discriminating preclinical strategy: Study paired pretreatment and post-cytarabine patient specimens, complemented by independently derived residual-disease models. Before treatment, classify samples by oxygen consumption and isotope-based de novo versus salvage pyrimidine flux under measured, physiologically relevant uridine and protein conditions. Include salvage-competent residual AML, untreated AML, and normal donor hematopoietic progenitors. Test concentration–time profiles bounded by independently verified human unbound exposure; measure intracellular drug exposure, DHODH inhibition, pyrimidine pools, and early metabolic changes before substantial cell loss.

Compare vehicle, teriflunomide, and inducible partial DHODH suppression, with uridine-rescue arms. A catalytically functional, teriflunomide-insensitive DHODH rescue construct, if independently validated, would strengthen target attribution; uridine rescue alone would establish pyrimidine dependence rather than unique target specificity. Include venetoclax–azacitidine as the established metabolic comparator [S3]. Track initially immature leukemic cells longitudinally using morphology, maturation-marker panels, and leukemia-associated genotypes, thereby distinguishing induced differentiation from selective survival of pre-existing mature cells. Assess apoptosis separately. After washout, measure clonogenic recovery and leukemia initiation by transplantation, rather than calling marker changes stem-cell eradication. Exposure-matched residual-disease xenografts should assess marrow pharmacology and propagation, alongside normal-progenitor colony formation and engraftment.

Alternative explanations include off-target cytotoxicity, reversible growth arrest, or selective elimination of immature cells masquerading as differentiation. Oxidative metabolism might mark chemotherapy stress without predicting pyrimidine dependence. Physiological uridine availability could also erase sensitivity observed in artificial culture. Temporal measurements, lineage tracking, genetic perturbation, and rescue distinguish these possibilities.

Falsification and limitations: A decisive falsifying observation would be confirmed DHODH inhibition and pyrimidine depletion at attainable exposure in preclassified salvage-poor residual AML, without differentiation or reduced leukemia-propagating capacity. Comparable impairment of normal progenitor function would reject the proposed selective window. Effects restricted to unattainable concentrations would defeat the translational hypothesis even if the cellular mechanism were supported. Sample heterogeneity, changing salvage capacity, transplantation biases, and uncertain marrow exposure limit generalization; positive preclinical results would not establish clinical efficacy.

proposals.title: Teriflunomide-induced differentiation in uridine-salvage-limited residual AML
proposals.text:
Teriflunomide-induced differentiation in uridine-salvage-limited residual AML

Hypothesis and evidence. In oxidatively active, cytarabine-persistent AML with limited uridine salvage, teriflunomide will induce DHODH-dependent pyrimidine restriction and leukemic differentiation, reduce leukemia-propagating capacity, and spare normal progenitors. Cytarabine residual cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties without consistent stem-cell enrichment [S2]; DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation in experimental AML [S4]. Neither establishes teriflunomide sensitivity or salvage dependence. ROS-low, BCL-2-associated stem cells represent a distinct context [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is an established comparator, not this repurposing intervention [S3]. De novo pyrimidine dependence, causal salvage limitation, differentiation instead of toxicity, and normal-cell selectivity are speculative bridges.

Drug and novelty gaps. Unverified prior knowledge: teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis and inhibits DHODH; uridine salvage can bypass DHODH-dependent de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Verify these claims, potency, selectivity, protein binding, and human unbound exposure against regulatory records and primary pharmacology studies before assessing feasibility. The packet cannot supply that verification; translational feasibility remains unresolved. Prior teriflunomide/leflunomide AML literature also needs checking, so novelty is unestablished. The discriminating prediction is that manipulating salvage reversibly changes differentiation at comparable DHODH engagement—not that DHODH-induced differentiation is new.

Operational context. Before response testing, use isotope tracing to define a salvage-reserve index: maximal uridine-derived pyrimidine-production flux across a measured marrow-relevant uridine range divided by basal total pyrimidine-production flux. Prespecify low reserve as ≤0.25 and high reserve as ≥0.75. These are design cutoffs, not validated biological boundaries; analyze reserve continuously and retain intermediate samples. Compare paired pretreatment/post-cytarabine specimens after cytarabine washout, independent residual-disease models, and healthy-donor progenitors. Include stromal coculture, measured extracellular uridine, and respiratory phenotyping without inferring stemness.

Exposure and mechanism. Set a concentration–time ceiling from verified human unbound pharmacokinetics and measured culture binding; supra-ceiling effects cannot establish feasibility. Compare vehicle, an orthogonal DHODH inhibitor, a mitochondrial-stress control, and venetoclax–azacitidine [S3]. Measure DHODH-pathway metabolites, pyrimidine pools, and flux before apoptosis. Require concordance with DHODH suppression, uridine restoration of pools with reversal of differentiation, and a biochemically validated inhibitor-resistant DHODH rescue in tractable models. Morphology and myeloid markers must identify viable differentiated cells carrying the leukemia genotype, excluding normal-cell enrichment or selective blast loss.

Causal context test. Uridine rescue alone cannot establish baseline salvage as a response modifier. Identify the limiting salvage step experimentally; increase its activity in low-reserve AML and decrease it in high-reserve AML, confirming changed flux and comparable target engagement. Use factorial vehicle/drug arms: increased reserve must attenuate drug-induced differentiation, and reduced reserve must intensify it. Prespecify an inverse drug-by-continuous-reserve interaction using donor-blocked analyses. Test residual status for additional predictive value after accounting for reserve and respiration; absent incremental value rejects residual status as an enrichment biomarker, not necessarily salvage dependence.

Endpoints. Prespecified success requires at least a 15-percentage-point increase in viable genotype-confirmed differentiated cells, increased absolute mature leukemic-cell numbers, and at least a 50% reduction in leukemia-initiating frequency after washout using equal viable-cell inputs. Measure clonogenicity separately from bulk death. Normal progenitor colony output and long-term engraftment must retain at least 80% of controls at matched exposure. These are experimental decision thresholds, not clinical surrogates. Use donor-level replication and a power calculation for the interaction; confirm activity in residual-disease xenografts only with measured, exposure-compatible marrow concentrations.

Alternatives, falsification, and limitations. Off-target injury, nonspecific mitochondrial stress, and selection of pre-existing mature clones could mimic benefit. Track initially immature leukemia-genotyped cells over time and apply target-bypass controls. Adequately powered failure to meet differentiation and leukemia-initiation criteria despite confirmed DHODH inhibition and pyrimidine depletion in prespecified low-reserve residual AML would reject the drug–context prediction. Validated salvage augmentation that restores pyrimidines but leaves differentiation unchanged would reject the causal modifier; benefit surviving target-resistant rescue would reject the target mechanism. Normal-function retention below 80% rejects the proposed therapeutic window at that exposure. Stromal salvage, inadequate free marrow exposure, specimen heterogeneity, culture-induced metabolic changes, and transplantation artifacts limit extrapolation. Differentiation may leave propagating clones intact. A positive result supports further development, not clinical AML efficacy.

proposals.title: Bedaquiline, an approved multidrug-resistant-tuberculosis drug, collapses ATP-synthase-dependent oxidative phosphorylation to selectively deplete ROS-low leukemia stem cells and cytarabine-resistant OXPHOS-high residual AML cells.
proposals.text:
HYPOTHESIS TITLE: Bedaquiline, an approved multidrug-resistant-tuberculosis drug, collapses ATP-synthase-dependent oxidative phosphorylation to selectively deplete ROS-low leukemia stem cells and cytarabine-resistant OXPHOS-high residual AML cells.

HYPOTHESIS STATEMENT
Bedaquiline (original indication: multidrug-resistant tuberculosis — recalled, unverified prior knowledge; approval program and restrictions must be checked) will directly inhibit mammalian mitochondrial ATP synthase (complex V) at clinically achievable exposure, collapsing ATP-linked respiration in the two OXPHOS-dependent AML populations documented in the packet, reducing functional leukemia stem cell (LSC) frequency, and retaining activity independently of BCL-2 level — making it a candidate complement to, not a substitute for, venetoclax-based regimens, which are comparators here [S3], not a discovery.

SUPPORTED PREMISES (packet)
A [S1]: Quiescent, ROS-low LSCs in studied specimens showed elevated BCL-2 and OXPHOS dependence; BCL-2 inhibition suppressed OXPHOS and targeted quiescent LSCs.
B [S2]: Cytarabine-resistant residual cells were not consistently LSC-enriched yet required oxidative metabolism (mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked) — a second, distinct OXPHOS dependency.
C [S3]: Venetoclax-azacitidine disrupted LSC energy metabolism (TCA/OXPHOS), providing a clinically benchmarkable comparator for OXPHOS disruption.
D [S4]: DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation, showing that metabolism-targeting can yield differentiation rather than death; S4 is a mechanistic contrast that must be empirically tested, not assumed absent.

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES (each with its discriminating number)
Bridge 1 (linchpin; recalled, unverified): bedaquiline inhibits mycobacterial F1F0 ATP synthase, and some reports recall mammalian ATP-synthase inhibition in a sub-micromolar potency range. Standard TB dosing recalls approximate total peak plasma levels of ~2-4 ug/mL with ~99.9% protein binding, giving rough free Cmax of ~3-7 nM (arithmetic on unverified inputs). The discriminating number to verify first: mammalian ATP-synthase IC50 divided by free Cmax. Engagement at clinical exposure requires IC50 at or below free Cmax; verified IC50 exceeding ~10x free Cmax renders Bridge 1 non-credible without unsafe dose escalation.
Bridge 2 (restated as a formal head-to-head prediction): direct complex-V inhibition should kill ROS-low [S1] and cytarabine-surviving residual cells [S2] regardless of BCL-2 abundance. BCL-2 dependence will be measured, not presumed: BH3 profiling quantifies antiapoptotic reliance, and venetoclax-rescue experiments define whether venetoclax actually fails in S2-type models (no packet source shows it does). The testable claim: bedaquiline retains >=EC50 activity in BCL-2-low/MCL-1-high or venetoclax-resistant models where venetoclax potency tracks BCL-2 dependence.
Bridge 3 (contested prior knowledge): normal quiescent HSCs are recalled to be glycolysis-biased, but complex V is essential in all cells and quiescent HSCs retain OXPHOS capacity, so selectivity is an empirical threshold, not a premise: a pre-specified >=5-fold differential EC50 (AML versus normal donor CD34+ cells) is the go/no-go criterion.

PRIOR-ART CHECK
OXPHOS targeting in AML is a crowded class: venetoclax is established [S3], and recalled, unverified complex-I inhibitor clinical programs reportedly met toxicity limits. The packet cannot rule out prior bedaquiline-in-cancer or AML reports; a novelty scan is part of validation. If prior AML work exists, the genuinely novel claim narrows to the BCL-2-independence/venetoclax-complementarity test, not the drug-mechanism pairing itself.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS
(1) Nonspecific mitochondrial toxicity equally affecting CD34+ cells; (2) cardiac off-target liability (recalled QT prolongation, unverified) rather than complex-V engagement; (3) a DHODH-like differentiation mechanism [S4]. Alternative 3 is now explicitly tested via a differentiation arm so it cannot masquerade as a killing-based positive.

DISCRIMINATING PRECLINICAL TEST STRATEGY
1) Metabolic engagement: dose-response OCR/ECAR and ATP measurements in primary AML sorted ROS-low versus ROS-high and in S2-type cytarabine-surviving residual cells, anchored to a concentration grid spanning ~0.2x-2x verified free-Cmax equivalents, head-to-head with normal donor CD34+ HSCs.
2) Target validation: inhibited ATP hydrolysis/permeabilized-cell ATP measurements in purified or permeabilized systems; binding-competition assays with oligomycin at the canonical F0 site; engineered resistance via the mammalian c-ring subunit ATP5MC1 (the analog of the mycobacterial c-subunit resistance locus; locus naming recalled, verify) in editable AML cell lines; rescue by ATP synthase overexpression. Orthogonal cardiac testing (hERG, cardiomyocyte function) defines the window.
3) Mechanistic discrimination: BH3 profiling plus head-to-head venetoclax dose-response in S2-derived residual and venetoclax-resistant models [S2 vs S3]; a parallel differentiation arm mirroring [S4] — CD11b/CD14 flow cytometry, morphology, and an orthologous DHODH-inhibitor comparator — distinguishes differentiation from OXPHOS-collapse killing.
4) In vivo: cytarabine followed by bedaquiline in PDXs versus a venetoclax-azacitidine benchmark [S3] at PK-verified exposure; residual burden, LSC frequency by limiting dilution, and normal-HSC chimerism. Pre-specified go/no-go: >=5-fold selectivity index, verified IC50/free-Cmax <=1, and significant LSC depletion.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATION
The drug-mechanism-context relationship is refuted if any of the following hold: verified mammalian ATP-synthase IC50 >10x free Cmax; no OCR/ATP suppression (or no killing) at <=2x free-Cmax equivalents; AML-versus-CD34+ selectivity <5-fold for bulk, ROS-low, or residual populations; BCL2-profiled killing pattern indistinguishable from venetoclax (no measured complementarity); or no residual-AML efficacy/LSC-frequency reduction at tolerated exposure in PDXs.

LIMITATIONS
All bedaquiline approval, dosing, exposure, protein-binding, ATP-synthase-potency, and cardiac claims are unverified recall requiring confirmation before any program. S1/S2 are model-derived and genotype-restricted; OXPHOS dependency may vary by subtype or prior therapy. Extensive tissue accumulation of bedaquiline (recalled, unverified) may decouple plasma Cmax from true mitochondrial exposure, complicating the selectivity arithmetic. Murine PK and protein binding may not translate. A positive result would position bedaquiline as an investigational complement to clinical comparators [S3], not an established regimen, and would require normal-comparator and cardiac safety evidence.

proposals.title: Phosphorylation of Nup98 at proline-directed sites amplifies nuclear-import failure after cytoplasmic TDP-43 assembly
proposals.text:
Phosphorylation of Nup98 at proline-directed sites amplifies nuclear-import failure after cytoplasmic TDP-43 assembly

This hypothesis is restricted to experimental TDP-43 proteinopathy. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies are the initiating lesion in this setting. Phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin Nup98 at proline-directed sites is proposed as the next, pore-intrinsic step that impairs nuclear import. Loss of nuclear TDP-43 and later cell death are downstream responses. The same order is not proposed for every sporadic or C9orf72-associated ALS trajectory.

Supported premises are limited to the supplied studies. Nuclear-pore and transport components associate with insoluble TDP-43, and disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cells, with related pore pathology in ALS tissue [S1]. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 can de-mix without conventional stress granules, accumulate in a phosphorylated form, mislocalize transport-associated proteins, and accompany import failure, nuclear TDP-43 loss, and cell death [S3]. Phosphorylation of TDP-43 in those assemblies is a modification of TDP-43, not evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation [S3]. Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA is linked to RanGAP mislocalization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons [S2]. Cellular stress can recruit transport factors into stress granules and impair transport, and altering stress-granule assembly changes that phenotype [S4]. Placed side by side, [S3] and [S4] support two routes to transport failure: a stress-granule-independent TDP-43-assembly route and a sequestration route.

Speculative bridges are not established by [S1]–[S4]. The substrate is assumed to be Nup98. Unverified prior knowledge: Nup98 is an FG-nucleoporin, and phosphorylation of FG-nucleoporins in mitotic systems accompanies loss of selective nucleocytoplasmic transport. A further assumption is that a proline-directed kinase induced after cytoplasmic TDP-43 assembly phosphorylates CDK-consensus sites in the Nup98 FG region in post-mitotic neurons and thereby weakens FG–karyopherin interactions. No supplied source names that kinase, those residues, or that interaction.

The causal order under test is cytoplasmic TDP-43 assembly, then Nup98 phosphorylation, then import failure, then nuclear TDP-43 depletion and death. Stress-granule sequestration of transport factors [S4] and repeat-RNA-associated RanGAP displacement [S2] are alternative routes. A third alternative is direct capture of nucleoporins and transport factors by TDP-43 assemblies, so the import defect associated with [S1] and [S3] proceeds while Nup98 remains unphosphorylated. A fourth alternative is that Nup98 phosphorylation is only a late correlate of cellular injury.

The discriminating preclinical test uses inducible neurons that form persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies, with a parallel stress that forms stress granules without those assemblies. The time series records assembly markers, stress-granule markers, Nup98 phosphorylation at the prespecified sites, Nup98 localization, a quantitative nuclear-import reporter, nuclear TDP-43, and death. Endogenous Nup98 is replaced by a phospho-deficient or phosphomimetic mutant confined to the assumed sites, and a kinase inhibitor is added only after assemblies are present. Concordant support requires four results: phospho-deficient Nup98 preserves import and nuclear TDP-43 while assemblies persist; the phosphomimetic slows import in cells that lack TDP-43 assemblies; post-assembly kinase inhibition lowers Nup98 phosphorylation and restores import; and blocking stress granules leaves both Nup98 phosphorylation and the import defect intact in the TDP-43 arm. A C9orf72 repeat-RNA culture is a boundary condition. Unchanged Nup98 phosphorylation there would show that the RanGAP-linked route in [S2] can impair import without this Nup98 step.

A falsifying observation in the TDP-43 model is absence of a rise in site-specific Nup98 phosphorylation before import fails, an unchanged course of import failure, nuclear TDP-43 loss, and death in the phospho-deficient mutant despite continued assembly formation, or intact import in cells that express the phosphomimetic and lack TDP-43 pathology. Phosphorylation is reclassified as a downstream response if it appears only after import has already failed and delayed kinase inhibition leaves import unchanged.

Limitations follow from the evidence boundaries. Kinase identity, residue identity, and the choice of Nup98 are assumptions, and amino-acid substitutions can disturb pore structure independently of phosphate. Acute experimental timing does not establish the sequence in human sporadic tissue or in every C9orf72 case [S1], [S2]. Rescue limited to one reporter would narrow the claim to that cargo. The design tests a mechanism and does not validate a treatment.
